analysis.one_liner: Sends $15 billion in cash and loan guarantees to airlines after 9/11 and pays guaranteed compensation to attack victims.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 96-1 on the day it was introduced, voided its own passage the next day, and the substance became law within days through a House bill.
analysis.plain_summary: Days after the September 11 attacks grounded every commercial flight, this bill gave airlines $5 billion in direct cash for their losses plus up to $10 billion in federally guaranteed loans, and had the government take over aviation insurance that private insurers had stopped offering. In exchange for capping what airlines owed victims of the attacks, it created the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund, which paid injured people and families of the killed a guaranteed award without a lawsuit. The Senate passed it 96-1 the same day it was introduced, then voided the passage the next morning so the House could pass an identical version, which became law on September 22, 2001.
analysis.who_benefits: Airlines received cash for ground-stop and post-attack losses, access to federal loan guarantees, delayed tax deposits, government insurance backstops, and caps on their liability for the attacks. People injured or killed in the attacks and their families could take a guaranteed government award with no need to prove fault. Small communities had their subsidized air service protected, and travelers benefited from keeping the air system running.

how_it_helps.text: Compensates air carriers $5 billion for losses from the federal ground stop and for incremental losses through December 31, 2001, with payments capped at each carrier's documented losses.
Authorizes up to $10 billion in federal loan guarantees issued by a new Air Transportation Stabilization Board, which may also take equity stakes so the government shares in carriers' later gains.

Creates the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund, paying anyone physically injured or killed in the attacks (or their representatives) without requiring proof of negligence, with payment due within 20 days of a determination.

Directs the Transportation Secretary to keep scheduled service to all communities, including $120 million for essential air service to small communities, and lets the government reimburse airlines for post-attack insurance cost increases.
Affirms $3 billion in spending on airline safety and security to restore public confidence in air travel.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the $5 billion in grants, up to $10 billion in guaranteed loans, insurance backstops, and the open-ended victim fund, all designated as emergency spending. Victims who accept the fund waive their right to sue the airlines and have awards reduced by insurance and other payments they received. Above a $100 million cap, the government rather than airlines pays for terrorism-related third-party losses.

drawbacks.text: Accepting the victim fund requires waiving the right to sue in court, awards are reduced by insurance and government benefits already received, no punitive damages are allowed, and the Special Master's decision is final with no judicial review.

Airline liability for the attacks is limited to whatever insurance coverage the carrier maintained, and for terrorism losses over $100 million the government pays the rest, shifting those costs from airlines to the public.

The victim fund's purpose is tied to protecting carriers: airline liability is capped only because the fund is the substitute remedy, and the exclusive federal lawsuit for the four crashes is heard in a single court.

Compensation paid to airlines under the act is taxable income, slightly shrinking the value of the aid, and government recovery depends on discretionary equity-participation contracts rather than guaranteed repayment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: In the days after 9/11, keeping commercial aviation alive and compensating victims had near-universal support, and the victim fund paid families far more than most lawsuits would have. The serious cost is on the liability side: airlines were shielded from the financial consequences of the attacks, with taxpayers absorbing losses above $100 million and victims trading their day in court for a government-administered award. The aid also included executive pay limits for carriers taking loans, which limited but did not eliminate the room for companies to spend the assistance as they wished.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 96-1 the day it was introduced, then voided its own passage the next day and indefinitely postponed it, so the House never voted on S. 1450 itself; the same substance became law days later through a House bill that President Bush signed on September 22, 2001.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Daschle on September 21, 2001, the bill was laid before the Senate and passed the same day without amendment, 96-1.
The roll call showed 50 Democrats, 45 of 49 Republicans, and the sole voting Independent in favor, with one Republican opposed.
On September 22, 2001, the Senate vitiated its passage and indefinitely postponed the bill by unanimous consent, pursuant to an order agreed to the day before, so the House never acted on it.

The bill's provisions—$5 billion in airline compensation, $10 billion in loan guarantees, aviation insurance backstops, and the victim compensation fund—became law within days as the Air Transportation Safety and System Stabilization Act, Public Law 107-42, signed September 22, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines were the clearest winners: the rescue money and liability caps they sought became law, and the Senate's voided vote cost them nothing. Victims' families gained a generous guaranteed compensation program, though it came bundled with the airlines' liability shield.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, with guaranteed victim payouts attached

sides.party_line_note: The Senate vote was 96-1: all 50 voting Democrats, 45 of 49 Republicans, and the sole voting Independent backed it, with a single Republican opposed.

industries.note: Carriers received $5 billion in direct compensation, up to $10 billion in federal loan guarantees, delayed tax deposits, and a government insurance backstop, which kept an transportation system everyone depends on running. Their liability for attack-related losses was capped at their insurance coverage with taxpayers covering amounts above $100 million, insulating them from the full cost of the disaster.

Private insurers largely stopped covering terrorism risk after 9/11, and the bill made the federal government the insurer of last resort for domestic aviation war risk while also reimbursing carriers for premium increases. Insurers kept collecting elevated premiums briefly but lost the market to the government backstop.

The bill channels up to $10 billion in federally guaranteed credit to airlines through private institutional lenders, who got a government-guaranteed outlet for loans to borrowers private credit markets would not serve. The government, not the lenders, bears the credit risk.
